blockMcqs.question: What core problem do polling, interrupts, and DMA all address?
options: How the CPU compiles code
How the CPU knows a device is ready without wasting cycles
How memory is allocated to programs
How caches stay consistent
blockMcqs.explanation: All three are strategies for handling slow devices without wasting CPU cycles waiting.

blockMcqs.question: Which bus carries the actual bytes being transferred?
options: Address bus
Data bus
Control bus
Interrupt bus
blockMcqs.explanation: The data bus moves the payload; address selects the target, control carries signals like read/write.

blockMcqs.question: What distinguishes PCIe from an older shared peripheral bus?
options: It removes the need for a data bus
Each device gets its own point-to-point lane
It only supports one device at a time total
It replaces memory-mapped I/O entirely
blockMcqs.explanation: PCIe gives each device a dedicated lane to a controller instead of sharing one bus with all devices.

blockMcqs.question: In memory-mapped I/O, how does the CPU reach a device register?
options: Special IN/OUT instructions only
A dedicated I/O bus with no CPU support
Ordinary load/store instructions
It cannot be reached by the CPU
blockMcqs.explanation: Memory-mapped I/O places device registers in the normal address space, so regular load/store instructions work.

blockMcqs.question: What is the main downside of programmed I/O (polling)?
options: It requires extra hardware
It cannot detect device status
It wastes CPU cycles spinning on slow devices
It only works with DMA controllers
blockMcqs.explanation: Polling repeatedly checks a status register in a loop, burning cycles while waiting for a slow device.

blockMcqs.question: In DMA, what does the CPU do during the actual data transfer?
options: Copies every byte itself
Polls the device continuously
Is free to run other instructions
Halts until the transfer finishes
blockMcqs.explanation: The DMA controller handles the transfer directly, letting the CPU do other work until one completion interrupt fires.

blockMcqs.question: When might polling actually beat interrupts?
options: When the device is extremely slow
When the device is fast and predictable
When many devices share one bus
When DMA is unavailable
blockMcqs.explanation: For very fast, predictable devices, a quick check can cost less than an interrupt's context-save overhead.

blockMcqs.question: Why does an interrupt handler save context before running the ISR?
options: To free unused memory
So the interrupted program can resume where it left off
To reset the interrupt vector table
To speed up the data bus
blockMcqs.explanation: Saving the program counter and registers lets execution resume exactly where it was interrupted.

blockMcqs.question: What does the interrupt vector table provide?
options: A log of past interrupts
A direct map from interrupt number to ISR address
The device's data buffer
A list of connected buses
blockMcqs.explanation: It's an indexed lookup, so the CPU jumps straight to the right handler instead of searching.

blockMcqs.question: Why doesn't DMA remove the CPU from I/O entirely?
options: DMA controllers cannot access memory
The CPU still sets up the transfer and handles the completion interrupt
DMA only works with port-mapped I/O
The CPU must copy each byte after DMA finishes
blockMcqs.explanation: DMA offloads the byte-by-byte copy, but the CPU still configures the transfer and reacts to its completion.
